body:
Nov 26, 2026 8:43am PT	
	

	
		Record Store Day Co-Founder on How Black Friday Evolved Into a Major Holiday for Vinyl Hounds, and What Will Fly Off the Shelves This Year
	

	The biggest shopping day of the year isn't just for big-box stores. Michael Kurtz predicts which artists, from Noah Kahan to the Beatles, will have LP enthusiasts up and in the shops early
	
			


			
			
	

									Record Store Day
	

		
	
				


	In April of this year, the 19th installment of Record Store Day was the event’s most successful ever, but Nov. 27 brings another opportunity for music junkies to get their vinyl on: Record Store Day Black Friday.

	While the O.G. Record Store Day was conceived as a general celebration of independent record stores, and features limited-edition, in-store only releases, the Black Friday edition exists for a different reason: to give those indie stores a slice of the “biggest shopping day of the year” pie. That’s also why the vinyl releases you’ll find making their debuts on Black Friday are more likely to remain there for the rest of the holiday season, and why many stores will make them available on their websites starting on Saturday the 28th.

	The concept of hyping local independent record stores as a must for holiday shopping may sound rather obvious, but RSD co-founder Michael Kurtz says that, at first, he was opposed to the idea, which his wife came up with.

	“I was not on board with it,” he admits. “My initial response at the time was, ‘Ah, that’s for big-box stores and selling cheap toasters and stuff.’” But eventually, he came around, thinking they could do “a little bit smaller version” for the holidays. RSD Black Friday does feature fewer releases overall, but its main goal is to get customers through the door. “Most record stores do about two months’ worth of business” that day, Kurtz says.

	For Black Friday, Kurtz says what you’ll find in the racks is largely thanks to what he calls a “Secret Squirrel group” of about 20 record store owners nationwide, who help winnow down the overwhelming numbers of releases pitched by artists and record labels.

	“They’ve been around forever; they run iconic record stores,” Kurtz explains of this crate-digging cabal. “And I go to them and say, ‘Hey, do you think record stores would want to have this?’ Because Black Friday is not the same as Record Store Day. It’s not supposed to be just a limited thing only. It’s also supposed to be things that record stores want to have in their bins year-round.”

	But what’s true for both events is that they feature releases from a dizzying array of artists across multiple genres. That big tent approach, Kurtz reveals, was inspired by Metallica bassist Robert Trujillo, who early on convinced Kurtz to do a vinyl release by iconic jazz bassist Jaco Pastorius.



	“It went to No. 1 on Billboard‘s jazz chart,” Kurtz recalls. “And that made us rethink: ‘Oh, geez, we could do jazz records, we could do bluegrass records, we could do soul records, R&B, funk.”

	Of course, rock in its various forms is still a huge focus of both Record Store Day and RSD Black Friday, but in recent years, pop artists have climbed on board the vinyl train en masse, resulting in a surprising boom in customers who are too young to even remember a world where vinyl was once the only option.

	Kurtz says, “The majority of people who come to Record Store Day now and participate are younger than the age of 35, and slightly more female than male.” Of course, you can credit the biggest pop star in the world for that.

	While Kurtz says Billie Eilish’s 7-inch releases for RSD “sort of cracked the door open” for that demographic, he notes, “It got blown wide open with Taylor Swift. When she did her ‘Long Pond Studio Sessions’ record with us exclusively for record stores [in 2023], it changed everything.” That album became the first Record Store Day exclusive release ever to hit the top 10 of theBillboard200, proving that brand-new releases on vinyl could do just as well as streaming titles.

	For RSD Black Friday 2026, Kurtz predicts that it’ll be Noah Kahan’s vinyls getting the youth through the door. “He’s got a special 7-inch that was done just for record stores that’s very very cool: It’s tied in with the ‘Hunger Games’ soundtrack,” says Kurtz, referring to “Draw You Out,” Kahan’s contribution to “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping – The Album.” “And then he’s also got an additional record that’ll be highly sought after.” That would be “The Last of the Bugs,” which collects the four tracks Kahan added to the expanded edition of his album”The Great Divide.”

	Kurtz is also excited about a Bruce Springsteen live box set, the American version of The Beatles’ Rubber Soul LP on gold vinyl, a live album by Billy Joel, a disc of the Doors’ studio sessions and a 2-LP set by Ween “for all the pot smokers out there.”

	He also predicts the Miles Davis, Jerry Garcia Band and Grateful Dead releases will be popular, as well as the original, previously unreleased version of Joan Jett’s “I Love Rock & Roll” album and not one but three albums by Japanese guitar virtuoso Masayoshi Takanaka.



	Kurtz says he doesn’t even mind that many of those younger customers are buying vinyl not to play, but to display.

	“Y’know, I was originally freaked out about that because I’m a music person, but I kind of get it,” he tells me. “Like, I will get the Beatles’ ‘Rubber Soul’ reissue this year and I probably will never open it. I just want it because it’s so beautiful, and to know that I have one of 15,000 copies that will ever be printed … I want to keep it pristine.”

	Despite admitting to being “completely anxiety-ridden” each year over how successful each Record Store Day event will be, Kurtz is looking forward to the event’s 20th anniversary next year. He and co-founder Carrie Colliton would love to mark the milestone with live performances and some kind of art installation featuring past Record Store Day releases. (A copy of each of those limited releases is currently stored in a warehouse in Raleigh, North Carolina, in case you might want to pull off the vinyl equivalent of robbing Fort Knox.) But for right now, Kurtz notes, those plans are “dreams right now. They’re not reality.”


	Still, the failure he fears is unlikely. Nearly 20 years into an event which has helped drive pop culture back to the vinyl age, Kurtz says there’s no sign of its popularity tapering off. As he notes, “demand for [vinyl] and the excitement around it is completely still there – even more so, I think.” But, he acknowledges, “The only thing that’s a bit alarming is how expensive it’s becoming” – a reflection of the rising cost of shipping due to increases in gas and diesel.

	“It’s stunning for me as a person who’s ridden this tiger called Record Store Day for almost 20 years to see it from the beginning: When we first started we were the only ones doing new vinyl, and in the used bins you could find [high quality copies of] Led Zeppelin or the Beatles or Pink Floyd for $3, $5 — those days are over.”


	Kurtz says it was interesting working with shops in the early days, and still can be today — because they’re independent in all sorts of ways, including what they prefer to emphasize in their stores and sometimes think RSD should focus on as a whole.
	

	“The most difficult thing about putting it together was working with record store owners, because they’re a very creative bunch,” he says. “They’re very different; they’re not people who typically play by the rules. They like to do things their way. So to try to get them all together to do this was very difficult.” He adds, “I was in London once and there was a record store owner who just just raked me over the coals because we’d done the Taylor Swift record. I was like, ‘What records do you like?’ He’s like, ‘Yes, Black Sabbath, Deep Purple …’ and I said, ‘OK I get it. That’s what you love and what you’re passionate about, but there’s another generation.’ And so it’s working with them and not alienating them, because sometimes I do that by accident.”


	
		More from Variety

title: BBC’s Antisemitism Crisis Represents an Unprecedented Chapter for the World’s Most Trusted News Organization
description:
It is a dark day for the BBC.

	On Thursday, government adviser Lord John Mann announced he is launching an investigation into alleged antisemitism
body:
It is a dark day for the BBC.

	On Thursday, government adviser Lord John Mann announced he is launching an investigation into alleged antisemitism at the broadcaster. It is an unprecedented chapter for the corporation, long held up as one of the most venerable and reliable media institutions in the world.

	For those who have been paying attention, however, the move is not surprising following a litany of public missteps dating as far back as 2021, when BBC News misreported an incident in which a group of Jewish students were attacked on a bus in Central London and then doubled down on it, despite eventually acknowledging the reporting lacked accuracy and impartiality.
	

	Later, the broadcaster steadfastly refused to reprimand Gary Lineker, one of its most high-profile sports anchors, as he repeatedly breached its much-touted social media guidelines, which were instituted precisely because of Lineker’s increasingly political Twitter activity. Under the guidelines, high-profile presenters hosting flagship programs are expected to be impartial while the show is on air and for a two-week window before and after. At the time, he called the guidelines “very sensible.”

	It was only when last year Lineker reposted an Instagram story about “Zionists” alongside a rat emoji that the BBC finally cut him loose. Even then, rather than a punitive measure, his exit was presented to the public as a mutually agreed decision for the host to leave after the final “Match of the Day” episode aired the following week. The BBC’s press release went on to call him a “defining voice in football coverage” and “thank him for the contribution he has made.”
	

	Critics compared the BBC’s apparently favorable treatment of Lineker to that of former BBC Radio 5 Live broadcaster Danny Baker, who was sacked immediately in 2019 after tweeting an image of a chimpanzee with the caption “Royal baby leaves hospital” just days after Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, gave birth, with the BBC calling it a “serious error of judgment.”

	The following month saw yet another incident when the BBC broadcast a little-known rapper’s rant about a former (apparently Jewish) boss, described alternately as a “fucking Zionist” and “bald-headed cunt,” before the crowd was engaged in a chant of “Death to the IDF.” It later emerged that producers had assessed the rapper as “high risk” and yet decided to broadcast his set live.

	Even as he embarked on his rant, which BBC chair Samir Shah later acknowledged consisted of “unconscionable antisemitic views,” no one at the broadcaster thought to cut the Glastonbury feed. Shah apologized for the oversight, and the BBC’s director of music, Lorna Clarke, briefly “stepped back” from her duties, although it appears little other action was taken (she has long since returned to her post).

	Then, last month, it was revealed that the BBC had reached an out-of-court settlement with one of its top factual producers, Lucie Kon, after she brought a legal claim alleging antisemitic discrimination. Kon, an Emmy and Oscar winner who exec produced “Mr Nobody Against Putin,” had worked for the corporation for 25 years but said that after Oct. 7, when Hamas murdered 1,200 people in Israel and kidnapped 250 more, the atmosphere toward her changed.

	The BBC rejected those claims but agreed to pay Kon £400,000 ($520,000) to settle out of court. For health reasons, Kon accepted. By comparison, the average award handed down by courts for race discrimination in the U.K. is £29,532, according to the most recent statistics.

	At the same time, the BBC’s reporting on Israel has been an ongoing source of contention. There was the Gaza documentary which failed to tell viewers the narrator was the son of a senior Hamas official, the report speculating Israel had bombed a hospital in Gaza which had actually been hit by a Hamas rocket misfiring and the news story in which an anchor misrepresented a Reuters story, saying the IDF was “targeting … medical teams as well as Arabic speakers” when in fact the medical teams and Arabic speakers were part of the IDF, there to assess patients on the ground.
	

	A leaked internal report last year — the same one that led to BBC boss Tim Davie resigning when it revealed the BBC had doctored one of President Trump’s speeches — noted that BBC Arabic, a part of the corporation’s World Service, had made 215 corrections and clarifications in its reporting of the Israel-Gaza war since 2023, amounting to two a week. At the time, a BBC spokesperson told Variety: “BBC News Arabic strives for the highest standards of journalism across its services.”

	(Incidentally, the BBC World Service currently operates in 45 languages, including Arabic, Amharic, English, Hausa, Kirundi, Marathi, Tigrinya, Ukrainian, Urdu and Yoruba. It does not include Hebrew.)

	So how did the BBC find itself embroiled in yet another crisis?

	Part of the problem stems from the fact that the corporation effectively marks its own homework. While British newspapers are regulated by an independent body, IPSO, the BBC operates the Executive Complaints Unit to investigate grievances about itself.

	But there is also a sense that the BBC, even under its new director general Matt Brittin, is not interested in engaging seriously with the issue. Each time there is a public blunder, the BBC will roll out the same playbook: issue a cut-and-paste apology (usually with reluctance), defend its reporting and make a gesture to suggest it has learned a lesson. But the sheer frequency of incidents — only a handful of which even spin out into the public realm — suggests nothing is being learned.

	Earlier this month, the corporation’s deputy director-general, Rhodri Talfan Davies, was asked during an on-the-record Q&A session with journalists whether he would support an internal inquiry into antisemitism at the BBC. His response was to deny there was a “deep-rooted issue” or any “institutional discrimination” at the broadcaster. Notably, he didn’t answer the second part of the journalist’s question, namely, if Talfan Davies didn’t think there was antisemitism at the BBC, “why do you think many of your Jewish employees think there is?”

	Even the corporation’s checkbox response to Lord Mann’s announcement on Thursday gives the impression, whether intended or not, that the threat of an investigation into its internal conduct is of little consequence. When approached for comment, a BBC publicist told Variety by email, “We’d also like to direct you to the below statement, that we’ve previously issued,” before literally copy-and-pasting it underneath.
	

	In his speech announcing the investigation, Lord Mann said he is “not interested in targeting individuals. That would entirely miss the point. I am targeting the institution.” The biggest clue as to the depth of the BBC’s antisemitism problem will be whether the institution even cares.

schema.headline: BBC’s Antisemitism Crisis Represents an Unprecedented Chapter for the World’s Most Trusted News Organization

title: Danny Boyle Backs Jack O’Connell as a Bond Villain, but Says He ‘Would Have Been Great’ as 007
description: Danny Boyle has thrown his support behind his “Ink” star Jack O’Connell as the man to battle Robert Pattinson‘s James Bond in the next 007 movie.
body:
Danny Boyle has thrown his support behind his “Ink” star Jack O’Connell as the man to battle Robert Pattinson‘s James Bond in the next 007 movie. 

	The director — who himself was due to direct the last Bond “No Time to Die” before leaving over creative differences — has acknowledged that with the lead role now cast, people had been “beginning to talk about Jack O’Connell as a possible villain.” 


	Speaking on the Alchemy with Anthony Mason podcast, he claimed that both O’Connell and Pattinson possessed a rare quality. “They have that thing [where] you want to watch them,” he said. “And it’s impossible to quantify what it is, otherwise we’d all buy it for ourselves. But it’s just there and you want to follow them.”
	

	However, he noted that O’Connell, who was believed to be among those considered for the role of 007, “would have been a great Bond as well.”

	As it turns out, back in 2019, less than a year after leaving the 007 franchise, Boyle actually suggested that Pattinson should replace Daniel Craig, having seen his performance in Claire Denis’ “High Life.” Speaking to The Guardian at the time, he said “It was so bizarre, because I was sitting there thinking: ‘Oh my God, they should get him to be the next Bond.’”

	Seven years on and with Pattinson finally anointed as the latest to join His Majesty’s Secret Service, Boyle noted that he could sense his capabilities for the role even further back. 

	“He’s a movie star, and I could see that from the first ‘Twilight’ films. Him and Kristen Stewart, the two of them. You thought: they’re movie stars. It’s like a given,” he said. “So there’s not that many of them out there. And having a British pedigree will always help him in that world as well.”

schema.headline: Danny Boyle Backs Jack O’Connell as a Bond Villain, but Says He ‘Would Have Been Great’ as 007

title: Mark Tildesley, Production Designer on ‘No Time to Die,’ ‘28 Days Later’ and Upcoming Beatles Biopics, Dies at 63
description: Mark Tildesley, the acclaimed British production designer who worked on major titles including the most recent James Bond movie “No Time to Die,” h
body:
Mark Tildesley, the acclaimed British production designer who worked on major titles including the most recent James Bond movie “No Time to Die,” has died. He was 63.

	Tildesley is understood to have passed away on Nov. 24 following a long illness.

	Across a career spanning more than 30 years, Tildesley collaborated with an array of leading directors both in the U.K. and beyond, on titles ranging from smaller indie films to big-budget Hollywood productions. Among those he worked with were Danny Boyle, Richard Curtis, Michael Winterbottom, Martin McDonagh, Mike Leigh, Paul Thomas Anderson, Cary Joji Fukunaga, Ron Howard, Ben Wheatley, Oliver Stone and Sam Mendes.
	

	Winterbottom would become a seven-time collaborator, with Tildesley working with the director almost back-to-back in the late 1990s and early 2000s on films such as “I Want You,” “Wonderland,” “The Claim,” “24 Hour Party People” and “Code 46.”

	Tildesley first joined forces with Boyle on his 2002 groundbreaking zombie hit “28 Days Later,” but the two would team up again on films including “Millions,” “Sunshine,” “Trance” and “T2 Trainspotting.” Boyle also tapped Tildesley as his designer alongside Suttirat Anne Larlarb for the 2012 London Olympics opening ceremony, a four-hour, wildly acclaimed extravaganza. It would win Boyle, Larlarb and Tildesley the Emmy for outstanding art direction for variety or nonfiction programming.

	With Mendes, he served as production designer on both “Empire of Light” and the upcoming “The Beatles — A Four-Film Cinematic Event” alongside Stefania Cella and Neal Callow.
	

	“Mark was a one-off: gentle, funny, warm, mischievous, entirely original and extraordinarily gifted,” said Mendes. “My abiding memory of him is from ‘Empire of Light,’ flying down the Margate seafront on a motorised scooter, his technicolored scarf flapping in the wind, twinkling like a schoolboy playing hooky. A unique spirit and a wonderful artist. I am one of hundreds of people who are desperately sad that he is gone.”

	Other credits include Leigh’s “Happy-Go-Lucky,” Curtis’ “The Boat that Rocked,” Lone Scherfig’s “One Day,” Bill Condon’s “The Fifth Estate,” Wheatley’s “High-Rise” and McDonagh’s “The Banshees of Inisherin.” With Fernando Meirelles he teamed on both “The Constant Gardener” and “The Two Popes.” Tildesley’s most recent credits were Noah Baumbach’s “Jay Kelly” and Joseph Kosinski’s “F1: The Movie.”

	“We are very sad to hear the news of Mark’s death,” said the British Film Designers Guild (BFDG), which awarded Tildesley three times (for “High-Rise,” “Empire of Light” and “F1: The Movie”). “Besides being a well-respected and extremely talented production designer, he was a friend and colleague to many of our members and will be very much missed by everyone in the Industry who knew and worked with him.”

schema.headline: Mark Tildesley, Production Designer on ‘No Time to Die,’ ‘28 Days Later’ and Upcoming Beatles Biopics, Dies at 63

title: Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Leads With $15 Million on Thanksgiving Eve, ‘Focker In-Law’ Earns $5 Million on Opening Day
description: “Sunrise on the Reaping” stuffed the box office competition ahead of Thanksgiving, generating $15 million on Wednesday. Fueled by positive word-of-
body:
“Sunrise on the Reaping” stuffed the box office competition ahead of Thanksgiving, generating $15 million on Wednesday. Fueled by positive word-of-mouth, Lionsgate’s “Hunger Games” prequel looks to collect $85 million over the five-day holiday period, which would push its domestic tally to $233 million. 

	Despite opening last weekend, “Sunrise on the Reaping” towering over two new releases. Disney’s animated “Hexed” earned $7.6 million from 3,725 theaters, and Universal’s comedy “Focker In-Law” grossed $5.3 million from 3,382 venues on their respective opening days. (“Focker In-Law” didn’t have Tuesday previews; showtimes began on Wednesday.) Although “Hexed” has pulled ahead on Wednesday charts, the fantasy adventure is projected to finish the weekend in third place behind “Focker In-Law.” Based on updated projections, “Hexed” is now targeting a five-day debut of $31 million to $35 million, while “Focker In-Law” is aiming for $35 million to $36 million over the same frame. Both films are falling short of pre-release expectations, which forecasted a $40 million to $45 million haul.
	

	Elsewhere, Netflix’s Brad Pitt-led “The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” brought in $910,00 from 252 Imax screens on Wednesday. The sequel to Sony’s “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which isn’t getting a traditional wide release, is expected to earn $4 million to $5 million by Sunday.

	In the case of “Hexed,” this opening weekend could spell trouble. That’s because the studio spent more than $200 million to produce the film, and theaters keep about half of ticket sales. So the studio needs the movie to resonate in international markets, and throughout holiday season, to justify the sizable prize tag. 
	

	Disney has long dominated the Thanksgiving corridor, and the studio’s animated sequels, namely “Moana 2” and “Zootopia 2,” are some of the holiday’s biggest earners of all time. Post-pandemic, however, Disney has struggled with original offerings, including 2024’s “Wish” ($31 million over its first five days) and 2022’s “Strange World” ($18 million debut over its first five days). “Wish” tapped out with $254 million worldwide on a $200 million budget, while “Strange World” left theaters with $73 million globally on a $180 million budget. What’s promising in this case, though, is that audiences seem to like “Hexed,” which was awarded an “A-” grade on CinemaScore exit polls. Positive sentiment should help the film’s box office longevity. The story follows a teen girl who discovers magical powers that take her from suburbia to Hexe, the world of witches.

	“Focker In-Law” also carries a sizable budget; Universal and Paramount co-financed the film for $90 million. Although theatrical comedies have become a box office rarity, the three prior “Focker” movies were notable box office winners. The original comedy of errors, 2000’s “Meet the Parents,” starring Ben Stiller and Robert De Niro as mismatched in-laws Greg Focker and Jack Byrnes, generated $330 million worldwide. The 2004 sequel “Meet the Fockers” is the highest-grossing in the franchise with $522 million worldwide, while 2010’s “Little Fockers” amassed $310 million worldwide. In this installment, Ariana Grande joins in the festivities the girlfriend of Greg’s son Henry (Skyler Gisondo) who meets the family as they gather for Jack’s 80th birthday party. Critics panned the film (a 29% on Rotten Tomatoes) but moviegoers have been more receptive; “Focker In-Law” holds a “B+” grade on CinemaScore exit polls.

	Despite the range of offerings, this Thanksgiving will fall short of cementing any box office records. Ticket sales are expected to hit $210 million to $215 million across all films in the marketplace. Thanksgiving 2024 was the holiday’s biggest on record with $422 million across all films, led by “Moana 2″ ($225 million debut), “Wicked” ($118 million) and “Gladiator II” ($44 million). Last year was among the top five with $293 million, boosted by “Zootopia 2” and “Wicked: For Good.” Theater owners aren’t discouraged because domestic ticket sales are already 20% above the same point in 2025. Plus, North American revenues are projected to surpass $10 billion for the first time since Covid upended the theatrical business.

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Leads With $15 Million on Thanksgiving Eve, ‘Focker In-Law’ Earns $5 Million on Opening Day

title: Gérard Depardieu to Stand Trial for Rape Charges After Failed Appeal
description:
French actor Gérard Depardieu will face a criminal rape trial after an appeal from his lawyers failed. 

	According to Reuters, on Thursday the Par
body:
French actor Gérard Depardieu will face a criminal rape trial after an appeal from his lawyers failed. 

	According to Reuters, on Thursday the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that a trial would go ahead regarding rape charges that stemmed from accusations made by actress Charlotte Arnould in 2018. She alleged that in August of that year, Depardieu raped her twice at his Paris home. He was indicted in December 2020 and has denied any wrongdoing. Last year, his lawyers appealed the prosecutors’ decision for the case to go to trial.
	

	Though the court rejected his appeal, it ruled that Depardieu will only be tried for the first alleged rape, and not the second. If convicted, the 77-year-old could face 15 to 20 years in prison.

	The news comes just 10 days after Depardieu’s withdrawal of a separate appeal regarding his conviction last year on sexual assault charges. He was given an 18-month suspended prison sentence for sexually assaulting two women on the set of his 2021 film “Les Volets Verts.”

	In a statement to French newspaper Le Monde, he said: “Justice has spoken. I have been found guilty. I accept this and take responsibility for this conviction,” offering his “deep and sincere apologies” to those who “may have suffered as a result.”

	Last week, a new complaint alleged further rape and sexual assault allegations against Depardieu during the filming of Guillaume Nicloux’s “Thalasso” in 2018. His lawyers told French radio station RTL that they were unaware of the complaint, which was filed in May 2025, shortly after his first sexual assault trial.

schema.headline: Gérard Depardieu to Stand Trial for Rape Charges After Failed Appeal

title: Qatar Is Forging Ahead With Film and TV Industry Plan, Undeterred by Regional Turbulence
description: Undeterred by regional turbulence, Qatar is forging ahead with its plan to build a film and TV industry that intends to put the tiny Arab state ric
body:
Undeterred by regional turbulence, Qatar is forging ahead with its plan to build a film and TV industry that intends to put the tiny Arab state rich in oil and gas on the global entertainment map.

	That is the main takeaway of the recently concluded second edition of the Doha Industry Days, held Nov. 19-21 during the Doha Film Festival, attended by some 450 prominent executives from 38 countries. 


	They included a robust contingent of Hollywood honchos, comprising Candle Media co-founder Kevin Mayer; Neon CEO and founder Tom Quinn; Mike Larocca, co-founder of Department M; Miramax boss Jon Glickman; Steven Paul, CEO of SP Media; and AGC Studios CEO Stuart Ford, to name a few. Most of them, in different guises, also serve as advisors to Hassan Al Thawadi, the lawyer who oversaw the 2022 FIFA World Cup and now chairs the Qatar Film Committee, the official body tasked with driving growth of the country’s entertainment industry. 
	

	Talents on hand included “Squid Game” creator Hwang Dong-hyuk, “Avengers” director Joe Russo, Omar Sy and Noomi Rapace.

	The Doha event took place despite regional instability caused by the U.S.-Iran-Israel war. In September Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Film Festival canceled its sixth edition that was scheduled to take place from Dec. 3 to 12 amid sharp escalation in its conflict with Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels, who had targeted several Saudi cities.

	“Obviously, you know the journey has not been easy,” Al Thawadi said in his concluding remarks, alluding to the impact on Qatar of the ongoing regional conflict involving the U.S., Israel and Iran. The conflict has delayed plans to shoot a Doha-set contemporary adaptation of William Shakespeare’s “Othello” that Oyelowo will direct and star in alongside Rachel Brosnahan and Cynthia Erivo, being produced by Barbara Broccoli that was announced during the Doha Industry Days last year.
	

	“But most of you are engaging with us; helping us build what we want to do,” he added. “And what we’ve got here, it’s a common vision, right? It’s not my vision; it’s not the Film Committee’s vision. It is all our collective vision,” Al Thawadi underlined.

	Al Thawadi went on to vow that next year’s edition of the Doha Industry Days “will be a lot bigger” and that, in the interim, there will more announcements, besides those that were made on the spot.

	Those announcements included concrete plans for a Neon-backed biopic titled “Caesar” about Syrian military officer Farid Al-Madhhan who blew the whistle on torture and killings perpetrated by the regime of Syrian president Bashar Assad; and two other still untitled biopics, one on Egyptian music star Mohamed Mounir, known as El King; the other on controversial Lebanese pop star Fadel Shaker. 

	During the event Qatar’s Film Committee also signed agreements with Egypt and Jordan, expanding the regional reach of the Qatar Screen Production Incentive, launched last year, which offers up to 50% in cash. The partnerships connect Qatar’s production incentives with cross-border collaboration, creating new opportunities to produce films across the Arab world.

	“The industry days here a year ago were something of a launch pad, where they laid out some broad parameters,” Ford told Variety during a wide-ranging interview in Doha. “And we’ve seen in the last 12 months, Hassan Al Thawadi and his team have started to put building blocks in place,” he said.

	LISTEN to an interview with AGC Studios chief Stuart Ford on Qatar’s ambition for premium Arab content on Variety’s “Strictly Business” podcast from Doha Film Festival

	“I think there is a very defined strategy,” Ford added, noting that Qatar has the benefit of starting to build an industry after the UAE and Saudi Arabia. “They are also coming to the industry at a time of great change globally, which creates huge opportunity for them to earn a place at the table,” the U.S. exec who has been long been active in the region went on to point out.

	“And I have nothing but admiration for the way that Qatar has, rather than just following tried and tested approaches of getting into the business, very much shaped a strategy around what Qatar is,” Ford continued. 
	

	“We’re seeing only the early stages of it,” Ford observed. “But this is a country of a couple of million people that, perhaps against most people’s expectations, hosted and put on an outstandingly well-organized World Cup.” 

	“So, in many ways, they’ve proven that they can execute on a plan, and I think you know they’re very likely to continue to make inroads into the industry in the next few years.”

schema.headline: Qatar Is Forging Ahead With Film and TV Industry Plan, Undeterred by Regional Turbulence

title: BBC Set to Be Investigated Over Antisemitism as Former Producer Says: ‘It Is a Hostile Environment for Jews Who Want to Be Openly Jewish’
description:
The BBC is set to be investigated over antisemitism.

	The government’s independent adviser on antisemitism, Lord John Mann, has written to the bro
body:
The BBC is set to be investigated over antisemitism.

	The government’s independent adviser on antisemitism, Lord John Mann, has written to the broadcaster to outline his investigation.

	“I am a big supporter of the BBC and public broadcasting. It is precisely because I believe in the future of the BBC that I need to intervene now and in this way,” Lord Mann said Thursday in a speech announcing the inquiry.


	The Labour Lord said he is not setting out to investigate specific reporters or programs but the “underlying atmosphere” that is hostile to Jewish staff.
	

	“The personal validations that I hear from former and current BBC Jewish employees and contractors is that fundamentally there is an institutional culture that demands that Jewish people must be expected to justify their existence, their identity, how they define their Jewishness,” he said.

	Citing a number of known BBC reporters including Jeremy Bowen, John Simpson, Feargal Keeane and Kate Adie, Mann said: “I defend their right to report. I am for free speech, not restrictions on speech. Including, by the way, when academics or others say things that I fundamentally disagree with.”

	“However, institutions that squeeze the space for its current and future Jewish staff and their voices and perspectives is the antithesis of free speech or fair and honest broadcasting.”

	Mann said he plans to speak in confidence to “every single Jewish employee or contractor of the BBC, past and present” as part of the inquiry.

	The news comes just weeks after it was revealed the BBC paid a settlement of £400,000 ($524,000) to Oscar-winning BBC producer Lucie Kon, who said she was bullied out of the broadcaster after raising concerns about antisemitism.
	

	Speaking to Times Radio on Thursday morning, Kon said of Mann’s proposed investigation: “I recognize those words completely and I know I’m not the only one. It is a hostile environment for Jews who want to be openly Jewish.”

	Last year the corporation apologized after broadcasting what chair Samir Shash acknowledged were “unconscionable antisemitic views live on the BBC” during a Glastonbury set.

	It also came under fire for failing to act after Gary Lineker, one of its highest-paid sports anchors repeatedly breached social media guidelines, including an Instagram story about “Zionists” that contained an image of a rat.

	Approached for comment about Mann’s investigation, the BBC directed Variety to a previous statement, which reads: “We take any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC. We have introduced compulsory training on antisemitism for all our staff and we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have.”

	“We are determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted.”

	News of the inquiry comes as the BBC is negotiating the renewal of its Royal Charter, which governs the broadcaster, with the government.

schema.headline: BBC Set to Be Investigated Over Antisemitism as Former Producer Says: ‘It Is a Hostile Environment for Jews Who Want to Be Openly Jewish’

title: India Targets at Least 10 Million AI Workers Through National AI Talent Mission, WAVES Film Bazaar Panel Hears
description: India plans to bring at least 10 million people into its AI workforce through the National AI Talent Mission, recently launched by Prime Minister N
body:
India plans to bring at least 10 million people into its AI workforce through the National AI Talent Mission, recently launched by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, according to Lt. Col. Vikram Singh Bhati, director of the National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET).

	Bhati was speaking at “AI and the Future of Creative Skills: Transforming India’s Media & Entertainment Workforce,” a panel at WAVES Film Bazaar, the market held alongside the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. Moderated by voice-over artist and actor Vijay Vikram Singh, the session also featured Amit Meena, director at the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship; K. Satish Nambudiripad, former director general of public broadcaster Doordarshan and chairperson of the Centre for Creative Economy and Public Policy at the National Institute of Technology Calicut; and Biren Ghose, founder and CEO of Astra Studios.
	

	“It started with the ministry launching a scheme called SOAR (Skilling for AI Readiness),” Bhati said of the government’s push to prepare workers for AI. He also called on companies to take part, saying “the industry should start absorbing people in the apprenticeship model” to help existing workers and new entrants adapt.

	AI is changing the production chain, from conceptualization to release, Meena said. “It is democratizing the whole process,” he said, stressing the need to reskill existing workers.

	Nambudiripad warned that AI tools “tend to homogenize,” and that “India’s folklore, regional languages and cultural nuances could be flattened” if training did not account for the country’s diversity. “You ask five people to write a concept note… if you are going through AI, every one of them will write the same,” he said. He called for technical institutions, film schools and industry to work together, and for skilling to reach India’s smaller tier-two and tier-three cities.
	

	Creative skills are shifting “from execution to imagination,” Ghose said, and from software proficiency to technology orchestration. “In the past we were wondering when the tools would catch up with us, and now we’re wondering when we would catch up with the tools,” he said. He also called for creative technology skills to be recognized in sectors beyond film and gaming.

	“No technology has ever invented anything,” Ghose said. “Everything that got invented has been invented by the ideas of man.”

schema.headline: India Targets at Least 10 Million AI Workers Through National AI Talent Mission, WAVES Film Bazaar Panel Hears

title: The Best Audible Books to Listen to Right Now: ‘ACOTAR,’ ‘Hunger Games,’ ‘Pride & Prejudice’ and More
description: If you’re looking to get through a few more books before the end of the year, now is a particularly good time to sign up for Audible. As part of its
body:
If you’re looking to get through a few more books before the end of the year, now is a particularly good time to sign up for Audible. As part of its Black Friday sale, the Amazon-owned audiobook platform is offering eligible subscribers three months of its Standard membership for just 99 cents a month, plus a $20 bonus to spend on audiobooks. The limited-time deal runs through Dec. 28. 

	Whether you’re looking for something to listen to on a long-haul flight home for the holidays or hoping to get a head start on your 2027 reading goals, Audible’s sprawling library runs the gamut from buzzy celebrity memoirs and bestselling romantasy novels to immersive, full-cast productions of literary classics. In recent years, the audiobook format has become an entertainment medium in its own right, with ambitious original productions featuring A-list voice casts, cinematic sound design and original music.


	From the latest installments in some of BookTok’s most beloved fantasy franchises to a reimagining of Jane Austen’s “Pride and Prejudice,” we’ve rounded up the best audiobooks to listen to on Audible right now.

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										BESTSELLER						

					A Court of Splintered Harmony		

	
		BookTok’s favorite romantasy author returns with the sixth installment in her bestselling “A Court of Thorns and Roses” series. Narrated by Elizabeth Evans, the long-awaited release kicks off a new story arc dubbed “The Valkyrie Cycle,” with the next installment slated to arrive in January 2027.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										BESTSELLER						

					Exoplanet by Andy Weir		

	
		From the author of “Project Hail Mary” and “The Martian” comes a cinematic Audible Original, co-written with Benjamin Percy and featuring a starry voice cast led by Anthony Mackie, Ariana DeBose and John Leguizamo. The sci-fi thriller follows the survivors of a spacecraft disaster who find themselves stranded on the same hostile planet across different points in time.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										BESTSELLER						

					Sunrise on the Reaping (The Hunger Games): A Hunger Games Novel		

	
		Fresh off its big-screen adaptation, the fifth novel in Collins’ “Hunger Games” franchise transports readers back to Panem 24 years before Katniss Everdeen enters the arena, chronicling a teenage Haymitch Abernathy’s fight for survival in the Second Quarter Quell. “Yellowstone” star Jefferson White narrates the audiobook.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										READ BY ROSAMUND PINKE						

					Sense and Sensibility		

		
	


			
			
			
			
	

	
					


						
			
	

	
					

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					Famesick by Lena Dunham		

	
		The “Girls” creator didn’t hold back in her long-awaited second memoir. In “Famesick,” Dunham recounts her tumultuous relationships with Adam Driver and her former best friend Jenni Konner, her fallout between her and Jack Antonoff and her struggles with addiction following her hysterectomy. Check out the biggest revelations from the book here.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					Roll the Calls by Ari Emanuel		

	
		Hollywood superagent Ari Emanuel opens up about his rise through the entertainment business in “Roll the Calls,” a candid account of building Endeavor and navigating decades of high-stakes deals, rivalries and relationships. The memoir also gets personal, covering Emanuel’s childhood struggles with ADHD and dyslexia, his marriage and family life and plenty of behind-the-scenes encounters with some of Hollywood’s biggest names.	
		
	

		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

										BESTSELLER						

					Daddy Issues by Sofia Franklyn		

	
		The former “Call Her Daddy” co-host tells her side of the story in a candid memoir that goes well beyond her highly publicized split from the podcast. Narrated by Franklyn herself, the book delves into the complicated intersections of fame, friendship, ambition and self-worth.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					Klara and the Sun: A Novel		

	
		Few novels feel more timely than Nobel Prize-winning author Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 bestseller, which explores the nature of human connection through the eyes of an AI companion purchased to care for an ailing teenage girl, played by Jenna Ortega in Taika Waikiki’s new adaptation. The audiobook is narrated by Sura Siu.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					Pride & Prejudice by Jane Austen		

	
		Harris Dickinson as Mr. Darcy? Say no more. Audible’s full-cast adaptation of Austen’s literary classic stars the “Babygirl” actor opposite “Industry” breakout Marisa Abela as Elizabeth Bennet, with supporting performances from Glenn Close, Jessie Buckley, Bill Nighy and Will Poulter, alongside an original score by Morgan Kibby.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					The Deal by Elle Kennedy		

	
		Elle Kennedy’s “The Deal” is the first book in the Off-Campus series, adapted into Prime Videos’ breakout new show about a hockey college romance. 	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					This Is Me: A Reckoning by Hayden Panettiere		

	
		In “This Is Me: A Reckoning,” the now 36 year-old actor recounts the traumatizing Hollywood experiences and tabloid scrutiny she experienced through the early-aughts, in addition to candid stories about postpartum depression, addiction and domestic abuse.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					Never Say Die by Ke Huy Quan		

	
		Quan tells the unlikely story of his Hollywood comeback in “Never Say Die,” beginning with his childhood as a Vietnamese refugee and early success in “Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom” and “The Goonies.” Quan also writes about the decades of rejection that led him to step away from acting, his work behind the camera and the eventual return that culminated in his Oscar-winning performance in “Everything Everywhere All at Once.”	
		
	

		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

					View from the East Wing: A Memoir		

	
		Jill Biden shares her account as First Lady of the United States for the first time in a new memoir — from her journey as a teacher to Air Force One, to a behind-the-scenes look at her husband’s bid for reelection. 	
		
	

		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

					Peculiar Stars by Rebecca Yarros		

	
		Described as a “slow-burn romance novel about love, family, and what it means to become the truest version of yourself,” bestselling author Rebecca Yarros’s newest book follows the main character Callista as she develops a relationship with her fiancé’s cousin in the aftermath of a tragedy. 	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					Remarkably Bright Creatures by Shelby Van Pelt		

	
		Now a Netflix film, “Remarkably Bright Creatures” follows grieving widow named Tova who forms an unlikely friendship with a remarkably intelligent giant Pacific octopus named Marcellus. The audio version is narrated by  Marin Ireland with Michael Urie as the voice of Marcellus.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					Project Hail Mary		

	
		Stranded aboard a spaceship with no memory, Ryland Grace, who Ryan Gosling portrayed in the blockbuster adaptation earlier this year, must piece together who he is, why he’s there, and how to save Earth from an extinction-level threat. Andy Weir’s signature mix of suspense, science, humor, and high stakes shines through in this interstellar odyssey. Narrated by Ray Porter, a standout voice in speculative fiction audiobooks. 	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone, Book 1		

	
		A chorus of more than 200 voices, ranging from young newcomers to Hollywood stars, bring new life to all seven of J.K. Rowling’s “Harry Potter” book series in a new production for Audible. The first audiobook in the bunch, “Harry Potter and the Sorcerer’s Stone,” dropped in November.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

										READ BY SHAILENE WOODLEY						

					Game of Nines by James Patterson		

	
		This high-stakes crime thriller drops FBI agent Sarah Cole into a chilling game: somebody has issued her an invitation to the “Game of Nines,” a secret murder puzzle that’s been baffling law enforcement for decades. Given one week to catch the killer — who promises to vanish and strike again in nine years if not caught — Cole must outthink a cat-and-mouse built for the most twisted of minds. Narrated in full audio-drama style by Shailene Woodley, Morena Baccarin, Sasha Roiz, and Ben Shenkman.	
		
	

		

						
			
	

	
					
		

					Semi-Well-Adjusted Despite Literally Everything: A Memoir		

	
		In this 11-hour self-narrated memoir, actress, dancer, and YouTube personality Alyson Stoner takes listeners through the twists and turns of growing up in the spotlight — the expectations, the struggles with identity and mental health, the pressure to perform, and the moments of self-discovery. 	
		
	

		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

					Robert Redford: The Biography		

	
		For those looking to revisit Robert Redford following the iconic filmmaker’s death this week, this biography traces his rise from youthful ambition to iconic Hollywood status while also unfolding his off-screen passions — from preserving the wild to championing new voices in film. Long before Sundance and screen legends, Redford’s story starts in small-town Colorado and arcs through acting breakthroughs, directorial risks and environmental activism. 	
		
	

		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

										READ BY MERYL STREEP						

					Heartburn by Nora Ephron		

	
		Meryl Streep narrates the audiobook version of Nora Ephron’s beloved novel “Heartburn,” which tells the story of Rachel Samstat who, seven months into her pregnancy, discovers that her husband Mark is in love with another woman. The  “Sleepless in Seattle” and “Harry Met Sally” creator reminds us all why she’s the queen of romance (and anguish) with this sidesplitting novel. 	
		
	

		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

										READ BY TARON EGERTON						

					Me: Elton John Official Autobiography		

	
		If you find yourself fascinated by Elton John after watching his upcoming documentary, you’ll want to read his debut autobiography in which the music icon himself narrates his remarkable life — from a young shy boy (born Reginald Kenneth Dwight) in a small London suburb, to the legendary artist who ended up changing the music world forever with his songs. Aside from his rise to success and extravagant lifestyle, all things shown in the bio-pic “Rocketman,” John also recounts his experience with the AIDs crisis and writes candidly about getting clean from addiction. 	
		
	

		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

										kate mckinnon and emily lynne						

					Heads Will Roll		

	
		Less of a book and more of an audio comedy, Audible Original’s “Heads Will Roll” is a 10-episode series created by “Saturday Night Live” star Kate McKinnon and co-creator/star (and sister!) Emily Lynne. The story follows Queen Mortuana of the Night Realm (McKinnon) and her ditsy sister JoJo (Lynne) who work together to hilariously put down an impending peasant rebellion that threatens their throne. The star-studded satire features performances by Meryl Streep, Tim Gunn, Peter Dinklage and “Queer Eye”‘s Fab Five.	
		
	

		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

					Just Kids		

	
		Patti Smith’s unmistakable throaty drawl adds dimension to the pioneering punk poet and singer’s exquisitely-observed and heartbreaking story of how she fled New Jersey in her early 20s, lived on almost nothing in New York, and moved in with photographer Robert Mapplethorpe while starting to perform at CBGB and Max’s Kansas City.	
		
	

		

			
			
			
			
	

	
					
		

					Crying in H Mart: A Memoir		

	
		The musician Michelle Zauner, known as Japanese Breakfast, proves she’s as adept at writing a sensitive memoir about family ties as she is at creating dreamy electro-pop. Zauner writes of growing up as a Korean American in Eugene, Ore., moving to the East Coast and beginning a band, and returning to Oregon to take care of her mother when she’s diagnosed with cancer. Memories of special meals she shared with her mother and grandmother and her efforts to come to terms with her family are woven throughout the book, which Zauner narrates herself.

schema.headline: The Best Audible Books to Listen to Right Now: ‘ACOTAR,’ ‘Hunger Games,’ ‘Pride & Prejudice’ and More

title: Alaska Woman Killed After Walking Into Spinning Plane Propeller at Airport
description:
Alaska Airport Horror
                          Woman Killed by Spinning Propeller
body:
Alaska Airport Horror
                          Woman Killed by Spinning Propeller
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 26, 2026
                            9:24 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              A horrific scene unfolded at an Alaska airport just 2 days before Thanksgiving ... a woman was killed after walking straight into a plane's spinning propeller.
      
    
              According to Alaska State Troopers, Christina Blake was driving on a taxiway at Big Lake Airport Tuesday afternoon when a small plane landed. The pilot stopped to give Blake room to move her car ... but instead, she got out, approached the aircraft and walked directly into its spinning propeller.
      
    
              Police, firefighters and paramedics rushed to the airport shortly before 5 PM ... but Blake was pronounced dead at the scene. The pilot was uninjured.
      

              Here's where things get particularly puzzling ... authorities say Blake had no apparent connection to the pilot, the plane or the airport, and investigators don't believe she intentionally walked into the propeller.
      
    
              Blake's body was taken to the State Medical Examiner's Office for an autopsy ... and the investigation remains ongoing.

title: Veruschka One of the World's First Supermodels, Dead at 87
body:
Supermodel Veruschka
                          Dead at 87
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 26, 2026
                            7:36 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
              Veruschka, the German fashion icon widely regarded as one of the world's first supermodels, has died.
      
    
              The legendary model -- whose real name was Vera von Lehndorff -- died Tuesday at her home in Berlin, surrounded by friends and family, according to German newspaper Bild.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Her sister, Catharina Kappelhoff-Wulff, confirmed her death in a statement on her fashion brand's website. A cause of death has not been disclosed.
      

              Veruschka shot to international fame in the 1960s, gracing the cover of American Vogue 13 times and working with some of the biggest names in fashion photography, including Richard Avedon.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              She also made her mark on the big screen ... appearing in the 1966 film "Blow-Up" and the 2006 James Bond flick "Casino Royale."
      
    
              Long before supermodels became household names, Veruschka helped define what it meant to be one.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              She was 87.
      
    
              RIP.

title: Donald Trump Blasts 'Lowlife' New York Times Reporter in Late Night Thanksgiving Rant
description:
President Donald Trump
                          Serving Up Thanksgiving Beef
body:
President Donald Trump
                          Serving Up Thanksgiving Beef
                          ... NYT Reporter Is a 'Lowlife'
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 26, 2026
                            5:49 AM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Donald Trump is kicking off Thanksgiving by carving up a New York Times reporter ... unleashing a late-night rant against the journalist before most Americans even got their turkeys in the oven.
      
    
              POTUS took to Truth Social at around 1 AM Thursday ... going off on veteran journalist David E. Sanger over an article examining a short-lived stock market rally involving tech giant Nvidia.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
              Trump accused Sanger of conveniently leaving out what he considers some of his administration's biggest accomplishments ... rattling off everything from border security and crime rates to tax cuts and military victories.
      

              But Trump quickly made things personal, writing ... "David Sanger is a lowlife that only writes what he is told to write by his bosses."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The president also managed to drag former President Barack Obama into his Thanksgiving tirade ... blaming his predecessor for a situation involving unstable explosives in Iowa that the Army recently detonated.
      
    
              For some context ... Sanger has been with the Times for more than 4 decades and has been part of 3 Pulitzer Prize-winning reporting teams.
      
    
              Trump wrapped up his post by boasting about his record on the world stage and the country's standing internationally.
      
    
              So much for a quiet Thanksgiving morning!!!
